Circle Through Circumcenter

GeometryTrianglesCircles
Game: This is a picture, not a game: a triangle sits inside one circle, and a second circle passes through two corners and the centre.
How to play: Drag the corners A, B and C, or focus one and use the arrow keys. Tick the boxes to show the names, the small circle, the right angle or the angle marks.
Look for the math

Move the corners of the triangle and the picture changes completely. One thing never does: the line from a corner to the centre of the big circle is perpendicular to the chord joining the two new points on the small circle.

Two circles and a chord

The dashed circle is the circumcircle of ABC: its centre O is equally far from all three corners. The solid circle is the one through B, O and C. It meets the line AB again at P and the line AC again at Q, so PQ is a chord of the small circle. X is where PQ crosses AO. The claim is that AO and PQ meet at a right angle at X.

Equal angles on the small circle

Angles standing on the same arc are equal. On the small circle, the angles ∠BPQ and ∠BCQ both stand on the arc BQ, so they match; and because Q lies on the line AC, ∠BCQ is the corner ∠BCA of the triangle. The same angle chase gives ∠APQ = ∠BCA. The logic test checks that identity on every triangle it tries. There is a small catch: if a second point falls on the opposite ray, the ordinary (unsigned) angle is the supplement of the directed one, so read the old page's chain of equalities with directed inscribed angles.

The central angle finishes it

In the big circle the angle at the centre is twice the angle at the edge: ∠AOB = 2∠BCA (or its full-turn complement when C is obtuse). Triangle AOB is isosceles, so ∠BAO = 90° − ∠BCA when C is acute, and |90° − ∠BCA| in general. Adding this to ∠APQ = ∠BCA gives 90°, which is exactly the condition for AO to be perpendicular to PQ. The check confirms the right angle on every acute and obtuse example.

What the checks found, and one exception

The logic test rebuilds the applet's own construction a second way from its bytecode and compares the two on 444 exact and generated triangles, including obtuse ones: AO ⟂ PQ in all of them, so the old page is right that acuteness is a red herring. It is not quite true for every triangle: if the angle at A is a right angle, then B, O and C lie on one line and no circle passes through the three, so the statement has no meaning there. When a secant is almost tangent, the applet's one-unit tie-break can pick the near intersection; the port uses the true second intersection, which agrees everywhere else.

Try dragging A towards the right angle: the small circle grows huge, and PQ stays perpendicular to AO right up to the moment the circle disappears.
